title: Saying Yes More Slowly Will Allow You to Say No More Often
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The problem taken up here is the regretted yes — agreement given from a wish to be helpful and liked, then repented at leisure. Rather than urging leaders to be more assertive in refusing, the piece inserts a delay mechanism: a list of ten clarifying questions to ask on receipt of any request, covering who else was asked, why this person, what is involved, what preparation is required, who will attend, and what happens if the request is declined. Two purposes are served at once. The questions buy deliberation time so that opportunity costs can be weighed, and they function as a screen — a requester who cannot answer them has revealed either that the request is unimportant or that the reader was selected as an easy target. The underlying economics are stated plainly: time is the only asset that does not grow or appreciate, so every yes forecloses other commitments, and the productive response is to be stingy with agreement.
points: The intervention is procedural rather than dispositional — a delay inserted between request and answer does the work that resolve alone fails to do.
The clarifying questions double as a diagnostic: inability to answer them signals an unimportant request or a reader chosen because they are an easy target.
Questions like ‘Who else have you asked?’ and ‘Why am I the best person to do this?’ surface the requester’s reasoning, which is usually where the weakness lies.
The opportunity-cost argument is put in asset terms: time is the only asset that never grows or appreciates, so each yes narrows what else can be given.
The author recommends treating a polite decline as a default good outcome rather than a failure of helpfulness.
quotes: But in their ambition to gain acceptance and please others, they sometimes say “Yes” to a request when they should have said “No.
With so much to do and so little time to do it, leaders need to get better at declining more requests and invitations so they can focus their time on what really matters.
Asking clarifying questions upon receiving a request can help leaders make better choices, ones they will be less likely to regret later on.
Be wary of those who can’t answer these questions. It likely reflects that the request is not that important or you are being asked because you are an easy target.
Slowing down the decision process before agreeing buys the time to consider all of the angles and consequences.
Whatever a leader says “Yes” to narrows the possibility of lending a hand with other invitations.
Knowing time is the only asset that doesn’t grow or appreciate, good leaders are stingy with what they agree to.
